analysis.one_liner: Taxes large investors one to five percent on each additional single-family home they buy, funding affordable housing programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 7 Senate Democrats, never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax companies and other investors that own more than 15 single-family homes each time they buy another one, with the rate rising from 1% to 5% as their portfolios grow. The money raised would go to federal affordable housing funds, and the minimum annual payment to states from the Housing Trust Fund would rise from $3 million to $7 million. New home construction would not be taxed, nor would nonprofits, governments, or community land trusts.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time and ordinary homebuyers, who would face less competition from large investors bidding on single-family homes in their neighborhoods [S3]. Low-income renters would also benefit: 65% of the tax revenue would go to the Housing Trust Fund, which funds affordable rental housing, and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, which finances affordable housing development, with the minimum Housing Trust Fund allocation to states rising from $3 million to $7 million [S3]. Small landlords, nonprofits, state and local governments, public housing authorities, land banks, and community land trusts would be exempt from the tax [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Discourages large investors from outbidding ordinary homebuyers by charging them 1-5% of the purchase price on each additional single-family home, with higher rates for bigger portfolios.
Directs 65% of the revenue to the Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, both of which finance affordable housing for low-income households.
Raises the minimum Housing Trust Fund allocation to states from $3 million to $7 million, so smaller states receive more funding for low-income rental housing and homeownership.
Exempts new construction, so the tax discourages buying up the existing housing stock without discouraging builders from adding new homes.
Carves out affordable-housing nonprofits, state and local governments, public housing authorities, land banks, and community land trusts, so mission-driven buyers are not penalized.
Includes aggregation rules that count affiliated companies as one owner, making it harder to split a large portfolio into smaller entities to stay under the thresholds.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and other investors owning more than 15 single-family homes would pay a tax of 1% to 5% on each additional home they buy, with the rate rising with the size of their portfolio: 1% for owners of 16-25 homes, 3% for 26-100 homes, and 5% for more than 100 homes [S3]. The revenue would flow to federal housing programs [S3]. Households selling homes to investors would not pay the tax directly, though sellers could receive somewhat lower offers if investor demand cooled [S3].

drawbacks.text: A purchase tax may not lower home prices if investor demand simply shifts elsewhere, and could reduce purchases by investors who supply rental housing in markets where renters rely on those units.
The lowest threshold applies to owners of just 16-25 homes, which reaches some small individual landlords and local family businesses, not only large corporations.
The tax targets only part of the affordability problem: it does nothing about housing supply, zoning, or construction costs, which many economists view as the larger drivers of high prices.
Funding for the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund would depend entirely on how much the tax raises, making the $7 million minimum the only guaranteed new money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain — less investor competition for entry-level homes, plus new dedicated funding for affordable housing — would fall on ordinary buyers and low-income renters, while the cost falls on a small set of large investors whose purchases drive up prices for the same buyers. The design is reasonably targeted: it exempts new construction, small owners, and mission-driven buyers, and its anti-circumvention rules close the easiest loopholes. The honest limits are that investor purchases are only one factor in high home prices, the smallest threshold touches some small landlords, and the housing funding is contingent on uncertain revenue. On balance it is a modest, well-aimed measure rather than a sweeping fix.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 25, 2024, with seven Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, and was referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee.

The only further congressional action was a Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee hearing held on March 12, 2024, related to the bill's subject matter; the Finance Committee, which held jurisdiction, took no action on the bill.
The bill never received a committee markup, a Senate floor vote, or House action, and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investors who own more than 15 single-family homes are better off because the bill never advanced: they face no new tax on buying additional homes, and the affordable-housing programs that would have received the revenue were not funded by it.

for.name: Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Sens. Tina Smith, Kirsten Gillibrand, Richard Blumenthal, Amy Klobuchar, John Fetterman, and Tammy Baldwin.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to this committee on the day it was introduced; the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, leaving it without a markup or vote.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to move a tax bill through committee and to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no floor action in the Democratic-majority Senate.

industries.industry: Institutional and large-scale single-family rental investors
industries.note: These investors would pay 1-5% on each additional single-family home they buy, with aggregation rules preventing them from splitting portfolios across affiliated entities to dodge the thresholds. The industry's interest in the bill runs against homebuyers, since its purchases compete with owner-occupants for a limited supply of homes.
New construction by any builder is exempt from the tax, so the bill taxes buying up existing homes rather than adding supply. Homebuilders could benefit as investor demand shifts toward new homes.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers, nonprofits, and community land trusts
industries.note: The Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund finance affordable rental housing and homeownership programs, and the minimum state allocation rises from $3 million to $7 million. Nonprofits, community land trusts, and land banks are explicitly exempt from the tax.
Small landlords and individual investors who own 15 or fewer homes are untouched by the tax, giving them a competitive edge over larger buyers. Those with 16-25 homes would pay 1% on new purchases.
